Mr. ST. LAURENT: It was not considered necessary to go beyond that. They are the employees who are making these copies for the purpose of keeping a record of a thing to be destroyed; and it was thought that if they made an affidavit that they had taken the photograph for the purpose of keeping a record of the thing to be destroyed, and that it had been destroyed, that sufficiently established that they were not making a trick photograph.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PHOTOGRAPHS OF BOOK ENTRIES ADMISSIBLE IN EVIDENCE
speechtext:
Should it not say when it was taken? Should the date not be given to show that it was taken in the ordinary course of business? An unscrupulous person could take a fake photograph and then destroy the document when some trouble developed.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That may be possible, but it was not considered that that was something that needed to be guarded against in enabling government departments or institutions to make microfilms of their records. One could conceive of a record being falsified. But this is for the purpose of enabling the compression of records into a smaller space.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PHOTOGRAPHS OF BOOK ENTRIES ADMISSIBLE IN EVIDENCE
speechtext:
I am not very favourably impressed with the method of furnishing proof by means of photographs. It seems to me that the legislation went as far as it should when it was confined to the original draft, and I think it is a dangerous precedent to set to extend that. There is a possibility, as suggested by some hon. members, that a document might, for example, have had an erasure or mutilation which was cleverly covered up, and a photograph probably would not show that erasure or mutilation.
In addition, it provides that any employee of the company may give evidence of the fact that it was a photograph of the particular document. An office boy in any one of these companies could give that evidence. It is conceivable that some minor employees of a company might collaborate in endeavouring to deceive the courts in connection with such a thing. Furthermore there is no question that the old method of cross-examination which has been the backbone of our judicial system for so many ages would be completely done away with, and in addition there is no provision- although I thought the minister suggested it- that an affidavit would be taken at the time and filed with the film in order that proof might be adduced at a later date. Take an instance where proof might be required five or ten or fifteen years after the photograph was taken; what person could give evidence of the taking of the film? Suppose all the employees had left the institution by that time. Certainly the provisions of subsections 3 and 4

could be materially strengthened to provide that an affidavit should be furnished and filed with each film at the time it was taken, and then a notarial copy of the affidavit could be used if wanted ten or fifteen years afterwards.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It must be realized that whoever destroys his original record is taking some risk. If he destroys a record and thinks he may at any time in the future be called upon to make evidence of it he is going to have this affidavit made at the time the original record is destroyed. That is the way it will work in practice. Those who are destroying records, in making their microfilms will file with the microfilm an affidavit of which a notarial copy can at any time in the future be produced to verify the correctness of the microfilm and enable them to make proof of it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PHOTOGRAPHS OF BOOK ENTRIES ADMISSIBLE IN EVIDENCE
speechtext:
A notarial copy by whom?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: A notarial copy of the original affidavit that will necessarily be made at the time the record is destroyed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PHOTOGRAPHS OF BOOK ENTRIES ADMISSIBLE IN EVIDENCE
speechtext:
The bill does not so provide.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If the hon. member were the manager of a company that was going to rely upon this film and authorized the destruction of an original record, he would certainly want to have, contemporaneous with the destruction of the record, the thing that would be evidence at any time under the terms of the measure, and he would require those who were proceeding with the destruction of the record to make the affidavit at once. He would not take the risk even of waiting until the next day to have the affidavit made.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PHOTOGRAPHS OF BOOK ENTRIES ADMISSIBLE IN EVIDENCE
speechtext:
On the other hand here we are extending to a person who wants to destroy an original document the privilege of substituting a form of proof in its place. We are not merely saying the substituted form of proof shall be prima facie evidence; we are saying it shall be admissible as evidence.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: As evidence of the thing it replaces, not as evidence of the facts.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PHOTOGRAPHS OF BOOK ENTRIES ADMISSIBLE IN EVIDENCE
speechtext:
But we are giving them the privilege of having that as evidence of the thing it replaces without any way of checking as to whether a comparison was made of the photograph with the original document, or when the affidavit was made. My opinion is that in this day and age we are getting rather loose with affidavits. With the present custom of requiring affidavits and declarations almost to the filling of your

Questions
individual teeth, the affidavit is becoming, I fear, a very common and rather sloppy method of proof. We are leaving the door open. We are not saying that the court may, in adjudicating on a matter, say, "I have some doubt on this, it not having been proven that a comparison was made with the original document and that the affidavit was made at the time that comparison was made".
We leave much to the vagaries of mortal man. In the case of the banks particularly, if a lawyer is filing a proof of probate he makes a notarial certificate that he has compared this document with the original one. He puts his notarial seal on it. The banks almost invariably insist upon getting the original probate as well as the notarized copy and comparing them before they will even accept the notarial certificate. So that if we were to deal with the request of those who ask for this legislation on the basis of the policy they themselves adopt, we would see at once the danger involved in granting their request. I submit we should proceed with extreme caution, and should at least require the filing of the affidavit almost immediately after the document has been compared with the original. Before it could be admitted as evidence, or even as prima facie evidence, such circumstances should be proven to the court.
Section stands.
